Moreover, the DMPO-1a and BHT-1a adducts could be detected by HRMS (Supporting Information). These results indicate a radical-mediated mechanism. The reaction was significantly inhibited by triplet-state quenchers, including oxygen and, particularly, the conjugated hexa-2,4-diene, suggesting the involvement of an energy transfer process (entries 5 7). Furthermore, the UV–vis absorption spectrum displayed a linear Stern–Volmer plot with a positive slope (Figure 3B), confirming the quenching the triplet TXO by 1a. Notably, the reaction of enantiopure 1a (>99% ee) proceeded with complete loss of chirality, suggesting rapid racemization of a carbon-centered intermediate (Figure 3C). To further elucidate the mechanistic details of the transformation, we conducted density functional theory (DFT) calculations with model substrate 1a (Figure 3D). DFT calculations reveal that photoexcited TXO ( \mathrm { E _ { T } } ~ = ~ 6 5 . 5 kcal/mol) efficiently transfers its energy to 1a ( \mathrm { E _ { T } = 5 2 . 2 \ k c a l / m o l ) } , generating the triplet diradical <sup>3</sup>1a via excitation of the C═C moiety. In contrast, excitation of the C═O moiety is precluded because its triplet energy (75.6 kcal/mol) is significantly higher than that of TXO, ruling out the Norrish-type reaction pathway under the present conditions.<sup>[52,53]</sup> On the triplet potential energy surface, <sup>3</sup>1a undergoes a 5-exo-trig radical addition to the carbonyl moiety via transition state TS1, with an activation Gibbs energy of 9.7 kcal/mol, forming a bicyclic intermediate <sup>3</sup>A. This pathway is kinetically favored over the competing 1,5-hydrogen atom transfer (1,5-HAT) process, which exhibits a higher activation Gibbs energy (12.1 kcal/mol). Subsequent C─C bond cleavage of the dirad ical species <sup>3</sup>A proceeds through TS2 with a low activation Gibbs energy (3.0 kcal/mol), generating an eight-membered diradical intermediate <sup>3</sup>B ( \Delta \mathbf { G } = - 1 3 . 6 \mathrm { k c a l / m o l } ) . Minimum energy crossing point (MECP) calculations were performed using the sobMECP software to estimate the minimum electronic energy required for intersystem crossing (ISC) during closure of ring-forming step. DFT calculations predict that the generation of cis-2 is favored, as the cis-configured MECP \left( \mathbf { M E C P } _ { c i s } \right) lies about 3.7 kcal/mol lower in electronic energy that \mathbf { M E C P } _ { t r a n s } , aligning with the experimental observations. Moreover, cis-2 is thermodynamically more stable than trans-2 by 23.5 kcal/mol, indicating that the severe strain in the trans-product drives thermal isomerization.<sup>[54,55]</sup> Accordingly, control experiments with products 22 and 27 ( \Delta \mathrm { G } = 1 4 . 2 ~ / 11.2 kcal/mol for trans-22 / 27 relative to cis-22 / 27), which were initially obtained as a 1:1 mixture of diastereomers, showed that the dr ratio remained unchanged when the mixture was stirred at room temperature for 12 h in the dark. However, upon heating \mathrm { t o 8 0 ^ { \circ } C } , excellent diastereoselectivity was obtained, in support of thermal isomerization of the highly strained trans-isomer (Figure 3E).

All calculations were carried out using density functional-theory (DFT) with Gaussian 16.<sup>[18]</sup> The geometry optimizations were performed with the ωB97X-D<sup>[19]</sup> functional using def2-SVP<sup>[20]</sup> basis set in DMSO using SMD<sup>[21]</sup> solvation model at room temperature. Frequency calculations performed at the same level of theory were used to classify each stationary point. Geometries without imaginary frequencies were deemed minima and those with only one imaginary frequency along the chemical path of interest were deemed transition states. Single point energies were carried out at the ωB97X-D / def2-TZVP<sup>[22]</sup> / SMD (DMSO) level of theory. To obtain more accurate Gibbs free energy (G) and enthalpies (H), we applied the quasi-harmonic approximation from Grimme<sup>[23]</sup> to compute the thermal corrections with a cut-off frequency of 1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { { c m } ^ { - 1 } } , thereby providing the final G and H in Shermo propram<sup>[24]</sup>. Minimum energy crossing points (MECP) were located using sobMECP program<sup>[25]</sup> interfaced with Gaussian 16. Conformational search using ABCluster program<sup>[26]</sup> was conducted to ensure that the conformers we reported were in their lowest energy conformation. The 20 conformers (if there are) with the lowest energy obtained from ABCluster were then optimized by DFT to determine the most stable conformer. The 3D diagrams of optimized structures were generated with CYLview20 software<sup>[27]</sup>.

computation_relevance: The authors computed substrate excited-state energies, a rearrangement energy profile, singlet/triplet crossing points, and cis/trans product energies for the exact model substrate. These private calculations directly address reaction feasibility and stereochemical outcome; distinct ΔG and ΔE values must be compared separately.

Other (hetreo)aromatic moieties including naphthalene (12),
thiophene (13), benzofurazan (14) and pyrimidine (15) efﬁ-
ciently underwent skeletal topological leap to provide the
corresponding CFMR in moderate to good yields. Notably,
an array of diene substrates was also successfully applied
to the skeletal editing and delivered the products 16 −20
successfully in moderate yields. Unfortunately, substrates A1,
containing an internal alkene moiety, and A2, bearing a
homoallyl group, did not undergo the desired transformation.
The inspiring results encouraged us to explore the ability
of the skeletal topological leap strategy for remodeling
various cyclic ketones into challenging CFMR architectures.
The substrate bearing two methyl groups at the opposite
α-position of the carbonyl failed to deliver the desired
product under the standard conditions, with the starting
material remaining due to the increased steric hindrance.
Gratifyingly, increasing the temperature could facilitate the
transformation, delivering the fused [5,1,0] bicyclic compound
21 in 60% yield. We next set out to examine whether the
protocol could be extended to larger ring systems. To our
delight, six-membered monocyclic ketone derivatives were
successfully converted into the corresponding CFMR frame-
works (22 −24) in 71%−80% yields. The results indicated
that the ester group is not essential, as its replacement
with phenyl or methyl groups did not signiﬁcantly affect the
yield, thereby expanding the potential modiﬁcation sites for
the diversity-oriented synthesis of CFMR. Moreover, this
ring manipulation is also applicable to more intricate fused
systems, yielding complex tricyclic products (25, 26) in mod-
erate yields. Notably, this skeletal topological leap strategy
could also be extended to seven- and eight-membered carbo-
cyclic/heterocyclic ketone derivatives, providing a convenient
access to the otherwise challenging fused [7.1.0] and [8.1.0]
bicyclic scaffolds (27 −29). Furthermore, a diverse array
of ﬁve-membered 1,3-dicarbonyl compounds bearing methyl,
ethyl, benzyl, and diphenyl substituent was proved compat-
ible, affording the corresponding products in good yields
(30–33), with no evidence of byproducts arising from 1,5-HAT
from the benzyl C–H bond. Cyclopentanedione derivatives
with benzyl substituents containing various functional groups,
such as pinacol boronate, ester, halogens (36–39) were also
competent substrates. The substrate bearing a long-chain
framework derived from citronellal shows little effect on
the reaction, affording the desired product 40 in 76% yield.
In addition, the benzo-fused ﬁve-membered diketone was
successfully transformed to afford the tricyclic product 41
under standard conditions in an isolated yield of 57%.
The six- and seven-membered 1,3-diketone substrates were
also suitable for the synthesis of structurally diverse CFMR
(42–46), revealing the generality and practicability of this
innovative strategy.
The value of this skeletal topological leap strategy
was further demonstrated through late-stage skeletal edit-
ing of complex natural products and bioactive molecules
(Scheme 2). Substrate 1at derived from norcamphor, bearing
a bicyclo[2.2.1] framework, was smoothly transformed into
a tricyclo[5.2.1.03,5] skeleton to furnish the desired product
47 in 99% yield. Likewise, substrates 1au and 1aw obtained
from carvone and loxoprofen underwent efﬁcient transfor-
mations to furnish the corresponding products 48 and 50,

rationale: The paper is a homogeneous small-molecule photochemical skeletal rearrangement with substantial author DFT and MECP calculations on an exactly identified substrate. Main Figure 3D, its prose discussion and SI S105 resolve the numeric OCR problem and distinguish free energies from electronic crossing energies. A coherent four-reference subset avoids the HAT prose/figure discrepancy. The public task contains neutral substrate/product structures and reaction conditions, with no triplet, radical, or ring-opening hypothesis.
reference_limitations: The 52.2 value is printed as 5 2 . 2 in the original extraction, but is visually 52.2. Figure 3D uses ΔG for this value; its electronic-energy difference is 56.8. Preserve that distinction.
MECP ordering is an electronic-energy comparison, whereas the 23.5 cis/trans product preference is a Gibbs-energy comparison. Neither is an isomerization or intersystem-crossing rate.
The HAT competitor is reported as 12.1 kcal/mol in main text and 12.2 in main/SI figures. It has been excluded from scoring instead of forcing exact agreement.
Product stereochemistry is part of the observed puzzle; mechanism, excited-state identity, radical pathway, MECP labels and author computation method remain private in autonomous mode.
SI S105 onward supplies methods, stationary-point energies and Cartesian coordinates. These exist even though the earlier extracted contract incorrectly described the coordinate evidence as absent.
scientific_question: For methyl 2-oxo-1-(2-phenylallyl)cyclopentane-1-carboxylate under the stated thioxanthone/395 nm irradiation conditions in DMSO, what accounts for rearrangement to methyl 5-oxo-7-phenylbicyclo[5.1.0]octane-1-carboxylate and the observed cis relationship between its C1 methoxycarbonyl group and C7 phenyl group? Develop and test a computational explanation.
